output.title: Exception queues before you automate
output.body:
Before you automate a workflow, look at the exception queue first. That is the work that falls out of the main process: customer questions that need a different answer, invoice mismatches, data corrections, or other cases that interrupt the day. If you cannot name the queue, you usually cannot automate it cleanly either.

The practical question is simple: which exceptions arrive often enough to deserve attention, and which ones are just one-offs? For one week, write down three things for that queue: how many exceptions appear, how long each one takes to resolve, and what rule the team uses to decide the outcome. Then sort the queue as routine, mixed, or ad-hoc.

Routine exceptions are the best candidates for a narrow automation pilot. Mixed queues still need human review built in. Ad-hoc work often stays manual, because there is not much pattern to work with.

Keep the control rules visible while you do this. If the queue touches approvals, thresholds, audit trails, money movement, or other high-risk decisions, human sign-off stays in place. Automation can organise the review, but it does not replace the person who owns the decision.

If the data lives in email, spreadsheets, or someone’s head, clean that up before you think about automation. A short, honest inventory of one exception queue is often the best next step.
